name: Erik Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what happens on your shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I tend circular knitting machines in a sock mill, replacing yarn cones and catching dropped stitches before a whole tube is spoiled. I finished secondary school and joined this row recently, so the mechanic still helps with difficult jams. The junior wage is low, but I like finding a fault before it spreads.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Naomi works at a school reception desk, and we have two school-age children, a mortgage and old debt from a failed decorating business. We have less than a month saved and few similar factories nearby. I use an AI fault helper every day, then write the fixes I have verified in a notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the knitting row that my daily AI fault notes still save me a trip to the mechanic for every dropped stitch. I would also say a camera cannot retie a broken yarn by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sock mill gives me paid shifts, but I am junior and the rate is low. Naomi’s school reception wage, our mortgage and two children leave less than a month saved, and my old decorating debt is still being paid down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep threading the circular machines and write the fixes I verify in my notebook. After a full paid month, I would make an extra payment from new wages on the decorating debt only if the mortgage and food are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, not the modest AI. A single stopped row can put the debt payment back into next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What fault did the AI note help with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It suggested a worn needle when the same stitch kept dropping, but I checked the needle before replacing it. The notebook records what actually fixed our machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much can you pay extra?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whatever the paid month leaves after Naomi and I cover the mortgage, food and school fares. I will not promise the lender money we have not earned.

say: I would tell the **knitting row** that AI notes help locate faults.
I would still **check the needle** before changing a machine part.
think: My **junior pay** and old decorating debt press on the household.
Less than **one month saved** leaves little room for a stopped row.
do: Keep **threading the knitting machines** and recording verified fixes.
Pay **extra decorating debt** from fresh wages only after essential bills.
feel: **Anxious** about baseline debt and the mortgage despite small AI change.
S0.quote: The notebook records what actually fixed our machine.
fieldNote: Erik already uses **AI fault notes** daily, so continued use is ordinary work.
His extra debt payment is **new cushion building** from pay, conditional on the family’s essential bills.

steps.text: Keep threading knitting machines and recording verified fixes
Pay extra decorating debt from new wages after essential bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a faster order book helps the mill only if the machines and people can deliver the socks. I would ask the boss to keep paid learning on the row instead of simply cutting a helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI planning might reduce the hours between batches, and a camera could take simple inspection shifts. I am still learning and low paid; Naomi’s school wage alone cannot carry the mortgage and old debt if my shifts shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my knitting shifts and test a new AI breakage alert against the notebook if the mill offers paid practice. After two reduced rosters I would apply only to a posted nearby textile-machine job that covers our bills, and I would hold off on replacing the family bicycle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like understanding a new fault, but I cannot risk the children’s food budget for an unproved system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the alert worth using?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would flag a broken yarn before a full sock tube is wasted, and the fault would match what I see at the needles. I would record false alarms too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. With less than a month saved, I need an offered paid practice place, not a private fee. An actual posted job matters before I spend time on another trade.

think: My **junior shifts** could shrink as planning and cameras change.

do: Learn the **new AI alert** only in an offered paid practice slot.
Apply after **two cut rosters** only to posted nearby bill-covering machine work.

feel: **Anxious** about lost wages despite interest in faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI could plan the mill in 2028 when I am forty five, but capable robots can tend the knitting row around 2031 when I am forty eight. We should see real fault records before management cuts operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most junior tending hours to disappear when robots can retie yarn and clear jams. The old decorating debt and mortgage remain, Naomi’s wage is too small, and less than a month saved will not carry us; I lie awake over that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid row shift while it exists, cancel the family trip and ask for the written staffing plan. If hours end, I would apply only to a posted reachable machine job at bill-covering pay with safe paid instruction; if none appears, I would ask my brother for short-term help with the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by losing most of the wage. I can make calls. Old debts do not pause for a new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a small knitting robot yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My old business debt is a warning about borrowing against a guess. I would need paying orders and a clear price before buying equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your brother be asked to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At most one mortgage payment while I search for a posted job. I would show him our budget first and not present family help as a permanent wage.

say: I would distinguish **2028 planning AI** from 2031 hands-on knitting robots.
I would ask for **real fault records** before junior operators are cut.
think: I expect **most tending hours** to disappear once robots can clear jams.
Old **business debt** and tiny savings make a wage gap dangerous.
do: Cancel the **family trip** and ask for written staffing figures.
Apply after **lost hours** only for posted reachable bill-covering work with paid safe instruction.
Ask my **brother for temporary help** if no adequate posting appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless debt worry.
S2.quote: My old business debt is a warning about borrowing against a guess.
fieldNote: His expected **large shift loss** and explicit sleeplessness warrant alarm rather than simple unease.
Past business failure makes him reject a **speculative machine purchase**, while any new job needs actual pay and safety terms.

steps.text: Cancel family trip and request written staffing plan
Apply after lost hours to posted reachable bill-covering job with paid safe instruction

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am forty eight, while capable knitting robots follow around 2034 when I am fifty one. Five years of paid work might be enough to clear some old debt and learn maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still cannot rely on the mill keeping junior tenders at fifty one. A maintenance qualification could help, but it needs paid practical time and a posted local job, or the mortgage will eat any savings first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the row shifts and pay extra toward the old debt from full months that leave a surplus. If the mill offers a fully funded maintenance course with paid workshop days, and a posted reachable maintenance role covers our bills, I would enrol and apply after qualifying only if safe isolation duties are written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can act before the physical machine arrives. I have learned from one failed business not to buy a promise with the children’s rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What repair would you need to practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified mechanic would stop and isolate a circular machine, then have me replace a worn needle drive. I would need an offered workshop place, not just a manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid knitting shift and the notebook. Naomi and I cannot trade wages for study until the course and the actual job route cover the household.

say: I would use **paid years** before 2034 robots to address debt and learn.
I would keep **2031 planning AI** separate from the hands-on change.
think: A **junior tender role** may shrink when capable robots reach the mill.
Maintenance helps only with **paid practical training** and a real adequate posting.
do: Keep **knitting shifts** and pay extra old debt only from fresh monthly surplus.

Apply after **qualifying** only with written safe isolation duties.
feel: **Anxious**, with time for a real paid route.
S3.quote: I have learned from one failed business not to buy a promise with the children’s rent.
fieldNote: He turns adaptive interest into a **funded practical course**, separately followed by a qualified job application.
Both moves require **offered paid time**, workshop access, a posted adequate local role and written safety duties.

steps.text: Keep knitting shifts and pay extra debt from fresh surplus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the row that thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am fifty three and capable knitting robots around 2039 when I am fifty six. Thirteen years before hands-on robots is enough to learn, but not permission to ignore this month’s debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children may be grown, but the mortgage and old business balance might still need my wage. A future robot date cannot tell me whether the mill has paid work, and today we have less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the paid knitting shift and make extra debt payments from full months with surplus. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would check rosters and posted nearby jobs; after two reduced months I would apply only for bill-covering safe machine work, while a funded paid maintenance place would be worth examining if actually offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current bills, though the longer warning gives me more chances. My last business taught me to count paid orders before buying a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you restart a sock business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if paying customers cover the equipment and rent first. I would not borrow against a forecast while the old decorating debt remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say learn a trade and read the tools, but check who will pay for the work. I cannot promise their first job from a chart about 2039.

say: I would tell the mill **2036 thinking AI** comes before 2039 hands-on robots.
I would ask workers to **count paid orders** before buying equipment.
think: The **mortgage and old debt** may still need wages at fifty six.
Our **thin savings today** make a distant timetable no guarantee.
do: Keep **paid knitting shifts** and add extra debt payments from new surplus.
Check **post-2036 rosters** and apply after two cut months only for posted bill-covering safe local work.
feel: **Anxious** about present debt, with time for measured choices.
S4.quote: My last business taught me to count paid orders before buying a machine.
fieldNote: His long-run scenario retains **today’s debt pressure** rather than assuming time erases it.
His later application is **conditional** on actual lost hours and a posted safe local job at enough pay.

steps.text: Keep paid knitting shifts and pay extra debt from fresh surplus

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could remove junior knitting hours around 2031 before I clear the old business debt. A funded paid practical maintenance place and a posted reachable job at bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the mortgage while a worker learns a different machine. A fault notebook can teach me a stitch, but it cannot pay the old debt.

headlineQuote: A fault notebook can teach me a stitch, but it cannot pay the old debt.
portrait: **Erik**, 43, is a junior sock-mill machine operator with secondary schooling and daily AI fault-note use.
His **low pay**, mortgage, two children, old business debt, thin savings and few nearby plants make lost hours serious.
He is **adaptive** about tools but refuses a speculative equipment purchase after an earlier business failure.
The fast case brings **expected major wage loss**; a longer runway helps only with paid practical training and a posted adequate job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut Erik’s junior knitting hours around 2031 before old debt is cleared.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded paid maintenance place** and a posted reachable bill-covering job would help him adapt.
